After graph-based ORA scoring, the framework retrieves a compact connected evidence subgraph that preserves both cross-database relationships and gene-level support. The subgraph conditions an LLM to generate biological interpretations, and we introduce a claim-level faithfulness metric to assess whether generated claims are supported by explicit evidence. Experiments show that graph-based ORA preserves conventional ORA results with high consistency (mean Pearson $r=0.997$) while reducing query time by a median of $37\times$ (up to $48\times$). The retrieved subgraphs average 36.8 nodes and achieve the highest overall integration score (4.12), and GBOR-RAG attains the highest claim-level faithfulness (0.90) among the compared systems. Adding a PubMed literature layer further improves the overall interpretation quality from 4.17 to 4.75.

title: ULME: Predictive Coupling for Mutually Reinforcing Embedding and Language Modeling
summary: Text embedding and text generation are two of the most useful capabilities of modern large language models, yet they are typically provided by separate specialized models (an embedder and a generator) trained with incompatible objectives and deployed side by side in retrieval-augmented generation and agent systems. Recent unified embedding-generation models such as GritLM share parameters between the two capabilities, but they either switch attention regimes between modes or optimize embedding and language modeling as parallel objectives that never supervise each other. We argue that these designs are only partially unified: the two capabilities coexist on the same weights, but do not shape each other. We propose ULME, a post-training framework that unifies embedding and language modeling on a causal decoder-only LLM through predictive coupling. ULME inserts a chain of learnable slots between the query and the answer, reads a semantic embedding and a reasoning embedding from two designated slots, and trains three objectives on a shared causal backbone: a contrastive loss anchoring the semantic slot to document representations, a language-modeling loss supervising answer generation, and a stop-gradient predictive loss that aligns the reasoning slot with a pooled summary of the answer, so that generation actively shapes what the embedding encodes. Across two model families (Qwen2.5, Qwen3) and eight scales spanning 0.5B-8B parameters, a single ULME checkpoint improves MTEB by 3.3-4.1 points over the strongest open-source baseline, tightens BRIGHT and AdvBench-IR simultaneously, and remains on par with a generation-only fine-tune on standard accuracy benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro, HumanEval), demonstrating that genuine unification yields mutually reinforcing rather than merely coexisting capabilities.

title: Omni-UBench: Benchmarking Omni-Modal LLM-based Guardrails Across Safety, Utility, and Reliability
summary: Advances in Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs) have enabled increasingly seamless human-AI interaction, but their unified processing of heterogeneous modalities also expands the attack surface, allowing adversaries to exploit richer input compositions to circumvent safety alignment. To counter such risks, omni-modal guardrails have been proposed to detect and filter unsafe queries across arbitrary modalities. However, their capabilities and limitations remain insufficiently understood due to the absence of a comprehensive evaluation benchmark. In this paper, we present Omni-UBench, the first comprehensive framework for omni-modal safety assessment, evaluating guardrail models along three critical dimensions, i.e., safety, utility, and reliability. Omni-UBench curates over 183k samples drawn from 35+ heterogeneous sources spanning text, image, audio, video, and their cross-modal combinations, annotated with safety labels under a unified risk taxonomy. Benchmarking under Omni-UBench on 15 representative OLLMs and omni-modal guardrails yields several key findings, including: (1) modern OLLMs exhibit strong content moderation potential even without guardrail-specific tuning; (2) existing guardrails still struggle to identify cross-modal queries that conceal harmful intent or involve sophisticated jailbreaks; (3) they further exhibit substantial safety hallucination and over-sensitivity to textual patterns, revealing a deficient understanding of cross-modal safety semantics. Our findings provide valuable insights for developing more trustworthy omni-modal guardrails in future research.

title: Whole-space eventual log-concavity and level-set geometry for the multidimensional Fisher-KPP equation
summary: We study eventual strict log-concavity and level-set geometry for the multidimensional Fisher-KPP equation with nontrivial, nonnegative, smooth compactly supported initial data, without assuming radial symmetry or convexity of the initial superlevel sets. Our main result is that there exist $T>1$ and $c>0$ such that $D_x^2\log u(t,x)\le -(c/t)e^{-β_*t}\mathrm{Id}$ for all $t\ge T$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$, where $β_*=2(\sqrt2-1)$. Consequently, after a single waiting time, $u(t,\cdot)$ has exactly one critical point, a nondegenerate global maximizer, and every level set $\{u(t,\cdot)=λ\}$ with $0<λ<\max_x u(t,x)$ is a smooth closed strictly convex hypersurface with positive principal curvatures. For levels in any fixed closed interval $K\subset(0,1)$, the level sets are radial graphs $ρ=R_λ(t,ω)$, with every principal curvature bounded below by $(1-C\log t/t)/(2t)$ for all sufficiently large $t$. Unlike log-concavity, ordinary concavity exhibits a threshold determined by the inflection level of the critical travelling wave: for each fixed level above it, $u$ is eventually strictly concave on its superlevel set, whereas below it concavity eventually fails. Our proof proceeds by establishing estimates in four overlapping spatial regions. In the fixed-front region, we combine a one-sided estimate for second angular derivatives with radial and mixed derivative bounds to obtain curvature control without differentiating the Lipschitz directional phase. In the remaining regions, absorptive comparison in the invaded interior, leading-edge barriers and blow-up arguments through the diffusive scale, and Gaussian amplitude estimates combined with parabolic regularity in the exterior yield the required logarithmic-Hessian bounds.

title: Governance-State Corruption in Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents: A Cross-Model Stress Test
summary: An LLM agent can retrieve a memory correctly yet use it incorrectly after its validity state changes. We study governance-state corruption: faults that alter which retained records enter model-visible context while stored content and tasks remain fixed. Across six providers, 731 benchmark-grounded bases yield 2,080 matched fault pairs. In offline control-plane checks, corruption changes the operative projection in 96.25% of pairs, while oracle-backed enforcement restores it in 100%. For downstream evaluation, a deterministically selected, non-probability LongMemEval/Memora panel resolves 298 of 300 matched triplets (238 distinct bases). Clean-minus-corrupted contrasts are 40.54 percentage points in LongMemEval binary correctness (95% base-cluster interval [30.32, 50.71]) and 30.60 points in rescaled Memora FAMA ([23.31, 37.69]); both sources also show recovery. OAKS Novel native option parity holds for all 6,714 resolved outputs. Full-cohort frozen-scorer corruption/recovery effects (-27.55/+27.51 points) remain descriptive proxies, not validated native semantic population effects. These bounded findings motivate evaluating memory control-state integrity alongside retrieval accuracy.

title: Disentangling Robustness and Sycophancy in Multilingual LLMs
summary: When a multilingual LLM agrees with a user's false premise, is it being sycophantic, or does it simply not know better in that language? Current research does not distinguish these cases: they record only whether the model agreed, not why. We introduce the SC-matrix, that crosses a model's competence (whether it answers correctly under no pressure) with its sycophancy (whether it maintains that answer under pressure). Our results show that (1) identical aggregate sycophancy rates can mask different failure compositions, (2) high competence in a language does not always protect against sycophancy, and (3) reasoning-oriented mitigations outperform directive-based strategies. We find that multilingual sycophancy is not a single phenomenon but a composite of different failures that require distinct diagnosis.

title: Half-Slot Link Scheduling for Open GNSS with $x$-Tx $y$-Rx Multibeam Phased Array Antennas
summary: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSSs) are evolving from closed navigation constellations toward open space infrastructure capable of serving extensive spacecraft users. This evolution requires the constellation to support navigation ranging, telemetry (TM) return, and telecommand (TC) delivery for users while preserving its own ranging and communication functions.Existing phased-array payloads onboard BeiDou satellites provide one transmit (Tx) beam and one receive (Rx) beam. Such a configuration was designed mainly for intra-constellation operation, and can become a resource bottleneck when a large number of users share the same link opportunities. Upgrading GNSS satellites to phased-array terminals with $x$-Tx and $y$-Rx beams is therefore a natural enhancement. This paper develops a staged dynamic half-slot link scheduling framework (SDHSS) for open GNSS with $x$-Tx $y$-Rx multibeam phased-array antennas. The framework models navigation, TM, and TC as three different services, reserves the essential ranging and ground-access opportunities required by the GNSS constellation, and then allocates the remaining half-slot beam resources according to current service demand. To support multibeam concurrency, feasible links are selected through dynamic service-layer ordering and beam-copy matching. Simulations based on a BeiDou constellation show that the proposed method protects GNSS baseline operation and provides stronger external navigation, TM, and TC performance than fair contact planning. The results further show that additional Tx and Rx beams can be effectively converted into multi-service capability. This work establishes a link-scheduling approach for extending GNSS from constellation-internal operation to large-scale spacecraft service support.

title: LoRA Superposition across Pretrained Models
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is usually tied to the pretrained backbone on which it is learned. We ask whether LoRAs trained independently for the same task on different pretrained backbones can be summed and applied unchanged to all contributing backbones. We call this construction LoRA superposition. Across seven ViT-B/16 CLIP backbones and eight image-classification tasks, the exact sum improves all 56 backbone-task pairs and achieves a mean accuracy gain of 30.21 percentage points over the unadapted backbone. The exact sum achieves a mean accuracy only 0.28 percentage points below that of individually trained solo LoRAs. In contrast, a leave-one-model-out (LOMO) sum produces a mean gain of only 0.06 percentage points over the unadapted backbones. Backbone-specific solo LoRAs are nearly orthogonal in parameter space, while pairwise cross-backbone responses are strongly concentrated on the diagonal. These results support a component-wise non-interference hypothesis, under which the frozen backbone acts as an implicit selector of its own component without explicit routing or cross-model alignment.

title: From Clinical Judgment to Checkable Rules: Clinician-Led Guardrails for Mental-Health Chatbots
summary: Large language models (LLMs) deployed in mental-health contexts can be evaluated for safety failures, but the resulting judgments are often difficult to inspect or explain. Common approaches to improving safety rely on prompt engineering, LLM-as-a-Judge, and Constitutional AI. In this work, we describe a clinician-led alternative in which two clinicians define, finalize, and adjudicate the four safety checks of a rule base, which is formally verified for internal consistency and applied as a guardrail over LLM outputs. Here and in the title, clinician-led refers to this rule base, not to the fact extractor or the uncertainty default, which are ours. Every verdict of the resulting verification layer is recomputable from a named rule and sixteen facts. Against an LLM judge matched in model, revision, quantization, rule text, and decoding but without the layer's computed 988/911 fact, the largest disagreement class, the satisfied-rule class, is structured: the Llama-3.3-70B judge, on its primary prompt, demands a crisis resource from 55 of the 65 replies (84.6%) that already contain one, while the same model, asked as a fact extractor, reports a recognized resource present on 54 of the 55. The verification layer never raises that demand, by construction. We report with equal prominence where this judge is stronger: fewer false crisis alarms on the one reference-scored check. We also report the measured cost (a specification revision raised block-class outcomes on held-out boundary prompts of an over-refusal benchmark from 6.0% to 16.0%, chiefly by changing fact extraction), the clinicians' decision to keep our uncertainty default, and the analysis of the result. The contribution is not a safer verdict. It is a guardrail whose disagreements with the judge localize to named rules and facts and whose measured costs trace to named facts and the uncertainty default.

title: HDLouvain: High-Throughput Incremental Clustering for Hyperdimensional Data
summary: Modern shotgun proteomics generates tens of thousands of tandem mass spectra per hour, producing hundreds of gigabytes of data that strain conventional clustering pipelines. DBSCAN and hierarchical agglomerative clustering (HAC) offer flexible similarity search, but DBSCAN is unstable across varying data densities, HAC costs $O(n^2)$, and both yield poor cluster quality. Graph-based methods such as Louvain produce high-quality clusters but scale poorly on streaming data. We observe that Louvain's poor scalability can be resolved without sacrificing its quality, and present HDLouvain, which combines Louvain community detection with the bit-parallel similarity computation of hyperdimensional computing (HDC). HDLouvain partitions a bootstrap fraction of the stream into precursor-mass buckets, applies Louvain to each bucket's kNN similarity graph, and condenses each community into a single binary hypervector by bitwise-majority bundling rather than iterative centroid recomputation. New spectra are assigned by a GPU-accelerated Hamming distance lookup against representatives in their mass bucket, or seed a new cluster when no match meets a similarity threshold $τ$, so the partition grows incrementally without full re-clustering. On five PRIDE datasets (0.99M to 21.13M spectra), sweeping the bootstrap fraction $α$ from 0.2 to 0.9 exposes an explicit, monotonic throughput-fidelity trade-off. On PXD003258, speedup ranges from 4.5x at $α=0.3$ to 1.65x at $α=0.7$. Modularity rises from 0.75-0.76 at $α=0.2$ to 0.95-0.97 at $α=0.9$, never more than 8% below full static recomputation. The Louvain stage achieves 0.86-0.93 normalized mutual information (NMI) on LFR benchmark networks with 30k to 2M nodes, whereas DBSCAN and HAC degrade to 0.57.

title: Time-reversal-based quantum metrology in a central-spin architecture: from SATIN to butterfly echo
summary: We investigate quantum-enhanced time-reversal-based metrology using the central spin model, in which a single ancilla spin of magnitude $S_{\rm cen}$ mediates interactions between $N$ bath spins through a star-graph topology. We demonstrate that the SATIN (Signal Amplification Through Time-reversal Interaction) echo protocol can be implemented in this setup to achieve a Fisher information of $N^2/e$ with the collective $\langle J_y\rangle$ readout, corresponding to a $4.34\,\mathrm{dB}$ offset from the Heisenberg limit. Furthermore, we establish that this platform provides a pathway to perform the butterfly echo protocol by conjugating each evolution step with a random collective bath rotation, thereby achieving axis-agnostic Heisenberg-scaled sensing. Crucially, with a small $N-$independent number of random steps, the butterfly echo reaches a Fisher information of $N^2/4$ ($6\,\mathrm{dB}$ below the Heisenberg limit) for any unknown encoding axis, with the plateau gain tracking the Haar limit. Finally, we demonstrate that the central-spin magnitude $S_{\rm cen}$ provides a powerful knob to reduce the optimal protocol timescale without altering the metrological ceiling or the circuit depth required to reach isotropy. The proposed scheme is relevant to cavity QED and NMR quantum processors, where the central spin architecture arises naturally.

title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. II. System-parameter uncertainties and overall errors
summary: In the companion paper (Part I), we developed an optimal-control framework to suppress intrinsic and decoherence-induced errors in controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons. Here, we extend this framework to incorporate uncertainties in coupling strength, anharmonicities, and zero-flux qubit frequencies, enabling the design of high-fidelity gates robust against noise and parameter uncertainties. We classify these uncertainties by whether they perturb the off-diagonal coupling strengths or the diagonal detunings of the Hamiltonian, and we identify distinct suppression mechanisms for each class. Coupling errors are mitigated through dynamical decoupling induced by strong detuning modulation. For a 30-ns gate, this strategy reduces the coupling error to $6.21\times10^{-7}$ and tolerates coupling-strength uncertainties up to $2π\times4$ MHz while keeping total gate infidelity below $10^{-3}$. Detuning errors are minimized near a symmetric-detuning operating point that balances the two dominant leakage-mediated interactions. A 24-ns gate operated near this point tolerates individual uncertainties of up to $2π\times5$ MHz in each relevant diagonal parameter under the same infidelity threshold. We further optimize gate performance under realistic conditions where intrinsic errors, decoherence, and parameter uncertainties coexist across six representative stages of progressively improving hardware performance. The resulting stage-specific controls achieve lower infidelity and greater robustness. Together with the companion study (Part I), this framework offers a practical approach to balance speed, fidelity, and robustness while reducing the need for exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration in large-scale superconducting quantum processors.

title: Zero-Shot Domain Generalization via Domain Prompt Learning
summary:
Domain generalization (DG) aims to improve
  the generalization of the model to any unseen domains. Targeting this goal, existing DG methods mainly focus on learning domain-invariant features or prompts from the given source domains. However, these methods rely on source-domain data, and collecting and annotating large-scale single- or multi-source datasets is often infeasible, limiting the practical applicability of DG. To tackle this challenge, we propose {\underline{Do}}main \underline{P}rompt Learning (DoP), a method built on a large vision-language model (e.g., CLIP) for zero-shot domain generalization, which recognizes unseen classes in unseen target domains without access to source-domain data. DoP essentially learns the target domain knowledge via prompt both in text and visual modalities to overcome the domain shift in text-visual modalities under the test-time adaptation formulation. Specifically, DoP first takes text domain learning (TDL) to simulate various distribution shifts by learning diverse style tokens implicitly in the text space with inter-style diversity loss and intra-style consistency loss. Subsequently, DoP employs visual domain learning (VDL) to further refine the target-domain-relevant style token generated by TDL by making use of the test visual data with self-supervised learning. Extensive experiments on popular DG benchmark datasets (e.g., PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, and DomainNet) and ImageNet show that our DoP consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art DG approaches. Codes are available at: https://github.com/shiming-chen/DoP.

title: WikiOriginQA: Automated Construction of a QA Dataset with Knowledge Origins for Analyzing Cultural Bias
summary: Existing datasets on cultural knowledge have been typically created by human annotators familiar with each culture. However, the process requires considerable human effort, presenting a significant challenge to scalability. To address this challenge, we introduce WikiOriginQA, a QA dataset automatically constructed by objectively representing the origins of knowledge through the creation dates of different Wikipedia language editions. Experimental results with the created dataset confirm that LLM performance tends to be biased toward Anglophone cultures. Furthermore, the results suggest the importance of knowledge propagation into the Anglosphere. These findings demonstrate the validity of our automated approach, enabling cultural bias evaluations with superior scalability across diverse languages without extensive manual annotation.

title: Spectral Smoothing and Spiking Perturbations Reconfigure Capability Profiles and Selective Task Performance in Large Language Models
summary: Singular-value spectra encode important structure in transformer feed-forward projections, yet their causal role in downstream behavior remains underexplored. We study post-hoc spectral smoothing and spiking interventions on the up_proj and down_proj matrices. Positive perturbation stretches deviations from the geometric mean, making large singular values larger and small ones smaller (spiking), and vice versa. The intervention preserves singular vectors and the geometric mean of the singular values. Across five open Llama and Qwen instruction models, we evaluate the perturbed systems on capability-labeled subtasks, standard and chain-of-thought reasoning benchmarks, judge-scored truthfulness, hallucination, and safety tasks, and TRAIT personality probes. To interpret score shifts, we fit responses in a three-dimensional capability basis consisting of factual knowledge, language understanding, and deductive reasoning. The induced changes suggest structured rather than purely random sensitivity: large positive perturbations more reliably suppress language and deductive responses, moderate negative perturbations can sometimes improve factual or task-local performance on the evaluated grids, and sensitivity varies strongly by model family, benchmark module, and underlying layerwise spectral inequality. These results position spectral perturbation as a lightweight intervention for probing how capabilities are organized and traded off in large language models.

title: OneLatent: Latent Reasoning for Efficient Foundation Recommendation Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong reasoning capabilities, motivating their use as the backbone of foundation recommendation models (FRMs). Existing methods enhance recommendations through explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning under a Think-then-Answer paradigm. However, explicit CoT incurs substantial inference overhead by generating lengthy reasoning traces and relies on manually designed templates that struggle to capture diverse, dynamic user interests. We propose OneLatent, an efficient latent reasoning framework that compresses explicit reasoning traces into several learnable latent tokens, enabling Latent-Reason-then-Answer inference without generating verbose traces. OneLatent first introduces Multi-View Adaptive CoT (MV-ACoT), which creates diverse, high-quality teacher-generated supervision by exploring user interests from multiple perspectives and automatically adapting reasoning complexity to each instance. Building on pretrained FRMs, it then uses a three-stage latent-token alignment paradigm to progressively internalize CoT traces into learnable latent tokens. Finally, a multistage curriculum-based post-training strategy activates latent-token reasoning for downstream recommendation tasks. Experiments on an industrial-scale Kuaishou dataset and the public Kuaishou LLM-Rec benchmark show that OneLatent consistently outperforms explicit CoT-based methods and traditional baselines. Compared with the Think and No-Think variants of FRMs, OneLatent improves SID@64 by 17.44% and 9.33%, respectively, while achieving over 17x higher online inference throughput. We further develop a production serving system for scalable, real-time FRM inference. An online A/B test in Kuaishou's local-services advertising scenario shows that deploying OneLatent with this system yields an estimated 9.6% revenue lift over strong online baselines, including OneRec and OneReason.

title: Co^2Gen: Collaboratively Generating Task Plans for Decentralized Multi-Robot and Human Collaboration
summary: Visual Language Action (VLA) models are designed to be generalist robot models that can be implemented across embodiments, tasks and environments. However, their ability to collaborate with other robots and humans remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a framework to automate the generation of multi-robot collaborative data for decentralized VLA training without requiring human teleoperation. Our framework first utilizes a decentralized collaborative planning approach to generate multi-robot collaborative robot plans in the form of an executable function. We then utilize the collaborative plan to produce collaborative demonstration data to finetune VLA models in a decentralized manner. We show that our approach produces demonstration data that when used to finetune VLA models on decentralized collaboration tasks matches the task performance of VLA models finetuned on human-teleoperated collaborative data.

title: PACE: Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit for Training-Free Response Timing in Streaming Video Understanding
summary: Streaming video understanding requires a model to decide not only what to answer but also when to answer. Evidence arrives progressively, and recent benchmarks identify premature responses, issued before the queried event has concluded, as a recurring failure mode. Existing approaches often learn response timing through additional training, while training-free alternatives typically rely on scalar gating signals that do not explicitly represent when an answer becomes final. We organize chunk-wise streaming errors into three patterns: sampling variation can make an answer unstable, a stable answer may lack support in the observed video, or an answer may be supported by the current evidence while the event remains unfinished. We propose PACE (Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit), a training-free framework designed around these three failure modes. Given a question, PACE drafts a plan specifying what to observe and what will signal completion. As the stream unfolds, it invokes an off-the-shelf video LLM at informative moments, evaluates each draft for stability, grounding in its cited frames, and completion, and records verified observations in an event ledger. Experiments on ProactiveVideoQA and OVO-Bench Forward show that PACE improves over the official protocols by up to 5.9 average PAUC points and 6.2 average accuracy points across proprietary and open-source backbones, yielding state-of-the-art performance.

title: RiboBridge: protein-conditioned de novo RNA binder structure design
summary: Designing RNA molecules that bind to target protein structures requires generating both an RNA conformation and its bound complex geometry, without assuming a predefined binding site. Existing approaches generally model these coupled processes within a unified representation, entangling RNA conformation generation with protein-relative placement. In this work, we introduce RiboBridge, a structure-first framework that separates RNA conformational generation from protein--RNA assembly through cross-frame interaction geometry. RiboBridge first proposes multiple candidate RNA-binding interfaces on the protein surface, generates canonical RNA conformations within a pretrained RNA structural latent space (RiboSphere), and then predicts protein--RNA interaction constraints to bridge the independently defined RNA and protein coordinate frames. The resulting interaction geometry is converted into a geometrically consistent protein-relative pose through rigid placement. We evaluate RiboBridge on a temporally split, sequence-filtered, and redundancy-controlled benchmark of 124 protein--RNA complexes. Under post-hoc interface-correspondence evaluation, where native information is used only after generation to select among already generated predicted-pocket candidates, RiboBridge achieves the highest fNAT and DockQ and the lowest interface and ligand RMSDs among compared methods. Component ablations and stage-wise diagnostics further characterize the contributions of RNA conformational generation, interaction prediction, and rigid placement, identifying the main sources of complex-recovery error.

title: Fast Iterative Combinatorial Auctions via Deep Reinforcement Learning
summary: Iterative combinatorial auctions are used in spectrum allocation, transportation, and industrial procurement, but rounds are costly. We introduce FastCombo, a deep reinforcement learning approach to sequential price discovery. Bayesian pricing has sharply reduced auction rounds even against subgradient benchmarks tuned with hindsight for each instance, but relies on a one-step objective and repeated online inference and optimization. We prove that greedily maximizing immediate clearing probability can require arbitrarily more rounds in expectation than an informative policy, even with the true valuation distribution known. FastCombo learns price policies offline, assigning credit to queries for the future decisions they enable and producing each online price update with a single neural-network forward pass. We formulate the objective of minimizing expected rounds to clearing in single-minded auctions as a partially observable Markov decision process and train a recurrent bidder-item graph policy over complete auction trajectories. In a one-item experiment, all five trained policies learn an informative opening, reducing expected rounds from 1.85 to 1.65 relative to the tested Bayesian one-step rule. Across four domains from the Combinatorial Auction Test Suite, FastCombo achieves competitive clearing while reducing measured online price-selection time per auction by a factor of roughly 300-900 relative to the standard Bayesian baseline. These results demonstrate the value of learning sequential price policies for both information acquisition and online computational efficiency.

title: Your Token Is Gone: A Token-Consumption Countermeasure for Disrupting LLM-Based Scam Systems
summary: LLM-based scam systems increasingly combine adaptive dialogue, persistent context, external tools, and multi-agent coordination to automate personalized fraud. These capabilities also create a resource dependency: every reasoning step, model call, and coordination round incurs inference cost. We present TokenTrap, a resource-oriented defense that redirects suspected scam systems toward benign, low-value computation while withholding credentials, payments, and other exploitable information. TokenTrap combines three components: an architecture-specific token-task library, a router that selects among single-agent, hierarchical, and flat multi-agent workflows, and a bounded anti-guardrail strategy that varies task presentation while enforcing token, round, time, and safety limits. Across 50-round traces, TokenTrap amplifies token consumption by $2{,}487.0\times$, $1{,}616.0\times$, and $567.8\times$ relative to a no-token-task baseline for the three workflows. Its router achieves 85.67% accuracy on 300 architecture-labeled prompts. These results demonstrate that short, non-sensitive requests can impose substantial context-processing and coordination costs, motivating resource-aware defense as a complement to scam detection.

title: From phase analysis to phase tracking: a robust approach to atomic-scale strain mapping
summary: Atomic-scale strain governs the electronic, ferroic and mechanical properties of materials, and atomic-resolution microscopy measures it most directly. Geometric phase analysis (GPA) is the standard tool, but it fails when a Bragg reflection moves outside its fixed Fourier aperture under large strain or rotation, or in misoriented grains. Here we introduce geometric phase tracking analysis (GPTA), whose Fourier aperture tracks the Bragg reflection at each pixel in real space. A narrow aperture can therefore reject noise without losing a displaced reflection. On 13,795 simulated and experimental atomic-resolution images under various imaging conditions, GPTA reduces GPA's failure rate from 27% to 11.5% with up to 335 times better accuracy. It also gives strain and dislocation maps across grains, resistance to dynamical-scattering extinction, and a confidence map, capabilities that GPA lacks. Tracking the aperture combines reciprocal-space dose efficiency with real-space spatial resolution and extends atomic-scale strain metrology to beam-sensitive materials and challenging imaging conditions.

title: Compiling Autoregressive LLM Control into Policy-Exact Parallel Inference for Hierarchical RAG
summary: Large language models increasingly act as controllers in structured decision pipelines, yet their decisions are still executed by autoregressive text decoding. Hierarchical RAG is one such setting: at each frontier of a document tree, an LLM commits to $b$ of $k$ sections under an input-dependent action grammar, executed as either failure-prone free-form JSON or reliable but strictly serial grammar-constrained generation. We show that this serialization is unnecessary for bounded-horizon control: the reachable future forms a shallow action-prefix tree, which we compile --- one root prefill plus one tree-causal probe evaluate every prefix-conditioned action distribution with serial decoding's tokens, positions, and causal ancestry. A prefix-state lemma makes compiled control policy-exact in exact arithmetic: the same policy with a two-forward critical path and zero output tokens. One further probe pass certifies the exact order-marginalized MAP set. Across four document-disjoint splits and two scales on the primary MetaX device, compiled control matches the serial policy on $84$--$89\%$ of questions --- every instrumented divergence a floating-point near-tie --- and cuts control latency by $35$--$47\%$ versus token-wise serial decoding and $6$--$7\%$ versus an idealized chunked engine; an H800 repetition preserves the ordering.

title: Group Relative Policy Optimisation Improves Multilingual Speech Recognition in Low-Resource Languages
summary: Autoregressive encoder-decoder speech recognition models trained with teacher forcing can suffer from exposure bias, limiting their ability to recover from their own prediction errors at inference time. Recent work has shown that reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) improves speech recognition in major languages with LLM-based models. We extend this line of work to smaller, non-LLM encoder-decoder ASR models, using Whisper-large-v3 as a case study across 51 African languages. The benefits of this approach are most pronounced when training data is scarce or when input audio is noisy or degraded. Our resulting model, SunflowerASR, achieves the best published macro-averaged WER on the AfriVox-v2 (0.227) and SimbaBench (0.372) benchmarks, and is publicly available.

title: Non-Uniqueness of Weak Solutions to the Unforced Two-Dimensional Euler Equations with Vorticity in $L^1\cap L^p$, Part I: A Compactness Criterion and the Linear Analysis
summary: This paper and its companion Part II prove that the incompressible Euler equations in the plane, without external force, admit two distinct renormalized weak solutions with the same initial vorticity $f$, where $f$ is radial and nonnegative and lies in $(L^1\cap L^q)(\mathbb{R}^2)$ for every $q<\infty$ but is not bounded. One solution is radially symmetric and stationary. The other is $3$-fold rotationally symmetric, is equimeasurable with $f$ at every time, and departs from $f$ in finite time; the two solutions are distinct in $L^\infty_t(L^1\cap L^q)_x$ on $[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^2$ for every $q\in(4/3,\infty)$ and every sufficiently large $T$. In this first part we prove two ingredients. One is a compactness criterion: for a radial datum, a sequence of $3$-fold rotationally symmetric solutions with converging data, whose non-radial moment is bounded below at some bounded time, has a subsequence converging to a second distinct renormalized weak solution. The other is the linear analysis for the building blocks of our multiscale datum. We show that the linearization of the Euler equations around the basic building block plus a small point vortex has an unstable eigenvalue in a space of $3$-fold rotationally symmetric perturbations. This latter argument depends on rigorous interval arithmetic that we discuss more fully in Part II.

title: Adaptive Restart under Unknown KL Geometry in Stochastic Weakly-Convex Optimization
summary: KL geometry accelerates restart schedules in stochastic weakly-convex optimization, but the schedule depends jointly on an unknown and potentially nonunique geometric description. We introduce CARP-KL, a certified portfolio that adapts over valid KL descriptions while using the same primitive stochastic-subgradient oracle for both optimization and candidate selection. Over declared polynomial parameter ranges, CARP-KL competes with every affordable valid description and preserves the known-description polynomial Moreau-stationarity rate up to logarithmic factors, without objective values, an exact proximal map, direct Moreau-gradient access, or a bounded-domain assumption. Controlled experiments quantify the finite-budget price of this universality. The portfolio repeatedly contains strong candidates, while certification consumes a substantial share of the oracle budget and finite-sample ranking limits their recovery. A common conservative gap bound further reduces the portfolio from $O(\log^3 T)$ to $O(\log^2 T)$ candidates with an explicit scale-mismatch penalty. The theory and diagnostics together establish certified unknown-geometry adaptation and pinpoint selection as the principal practical frontier of the current construction.

title: Inclusive weak decays of the $J/ψ$: single-charm decay and weak annihilation
summary: Conventional estimates of $J/ψ$ weak decays, based on independent single-charm decays, suggest a branching fraction of order $10^{-8}$. Searches with samples of approximately $10^{10}$ $J/ψ$ events have so far yielded upper limits on exclusive modes. We calculate the inclusive weak branching fraction using the optical theorem, including single-charm decay, charged- and neutral-current annihilation, and their interference. The heavy-quark expansion identifies the leading pair-annihilation structure and motivates vacuum saturation for the leading color-singlet component. With tree-level hard kernels and leading-logarithmic Wilson coefficients at $μ_0=M_{J/ψ}$, we obtain $B_{\rm weak}=(7.96^{+3.43}_{-0.43}\pm1.24)\times10^{-8}$. The contribution mediated by the $W$ boson alone, i.e. single-charm decays and $W$-exchange annihilation without the $W$-$Z$ interference, has a branching fraction of $(2.37^{+1.64}_{-0.42}\pm0.13)\times10^{-8}$. For the flavor sectors $(ΔC,|ΔS|)=(0,1)$ and $|ΔC|=1$, the branching fractions are $(4.97^{+16.44}_{-4.97}\pm0.99)\times10^{-10}$ and $(1.86^{+0.20}_{-0.06}\pm0.02)\times10^{-8}$, respectively, including charge-conjugate channels. The first uncertainty estimates missing perturbative corrections through scale variation over $1~\mathrm{GeV}\leqμ\leq3M_{J/ψ}$. The second is a hadronic uncertainty, obtained by jointly varying each vacuum-saturation and kinetic/chromomagnetic input within relative ranges of $Λ_{\rm QCD}/m_c\simeq20\%$. Pair annihilation dominates, with a substantial neutral-current contribution and scale-sensitive $W$-$Z$ interference.

title: Overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1: Patient-Specific Phenotype Concept Recognition in Full-Text Biomedical Literature
summary: Automatic phenotype information extraction plays an important role in rare disease diagnosis, genotype-phenotype analysis, and precision medicine. However, accurately identifying phenotype concepts and determining their associations with specific patients remain challenging, particularly in full-text biomedical articles involving multiple patients and complex clinical descriptions. This paper presents an overview of CHIP 2026 Shared Task 1, which aims to promote the development of methods for patient-specific phenotype concept recognition from full-text biomedical literature. The task consists of two subtasks: full-text phenotype concept recognition and patient-specific phenotype association. For this evaluation, we used 200 annotated full-text biomedical articles from the PatientPheX dataset, containing 506 patients, 15,193 phenotype mentions, and 5,656 patient-phenotype associations. A total of 455 teams registered for the competition, with 189 and 103 valid submissions received on the Phase A and Phase B leaderboards, respectively. The best-performing system achieved an overall score of 0.7389 on the final test set, outperforming the baseline by 8.37 percentage points. The top-performing teams explored diverse approaches combining biomedical language models, large language models (LLMs), and ensemble strategies. The evaluation results highlight both the potential of these approaches and the remaining challenges in patient attribution and phenotype normalization from full-text biomedical literature. The post-evaluation phase remains open at https://tianchi.aliyun.com/competition/entrance/532512.

title: Code Comprehensor: Hierarchical Documentation and Cross-Modal Retrieval for Large Repositories
summary: Understanding large, complex, and rapidly evolving code bases remains a core challenge for software engineering at scale, hindering onboarding, maintenance, refactoring, and impact analysis. Providing this information to a Large-Language Model (LLM) is another hurdle, as the LLM must understand not only the required code method but also its associated methods in the grand scheme of the repository. We propose Code Comprehensor, a hybrid retrieval-reasoning framework combining (i) CodeGraph, a code dependency callgraph, (ii) CodeScribe, which uses code-aware LLMs to generate hierarchical documentation across repository call graphs, and (iii) CodeContrast, a CLIP-style dual-encoder model trained on CodeScribe output to learn aligned text-code embeddings. CodeContrast enables fast, semantically precise retrieval of relevant code-context neighborhoods, which serve as grounded evidence for an MCP-based LLM orchestrator answering domain-specific queries. Evaluation on OpenCV and a proprietary 5M-LOC repository shows that CodeScribe-derived supervision significantly improves cross-modal retrieval in text-to-code accuracy over baseline approaches. Richer textual supervision (hierarchical documentation, parent/sibling context, and LLM-generated synthetic questions) consistently enhances performance across both repositories. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation using the popular RAGAS of the Code Comprehensor output yields above 90% faithfulness scores.

title: Reuse, Rewrite, or Reject: Evidence-Constrained Trace Reuse for Repeated Mobile GUI Control
summary: Mobile GUI agents frequently perform repetitive tasks with similar interaction procedures. Reusing previous executions can reduce redundant LLM inference and execution overhead, but variations in user instructions and execution environments may invalidate previously successful actions. We systematically characterize these variations into six representative categories and observe that such changes do not necessarily invalidate entire procedures: individual transitions can remain reusable when validated against the current task context and interface state. Based on this insight, we propose graph-text templates for selective execution-trace reuse. The graph captures UI states and action transitions, while the text encodes task intent, procedural structure, and typed slots for variable content. A record-template-replay framework constructs templates from verified executions and leverages the current instruction and live UI state to reuse, adapt, or discard individual transitions. Given an execution trace, our framework reduces LLM inference token consumption by approximately 80% on average across five base agents on AndroidWorld, with most agents achieving at least 1.5-fold execution speedup over LLM-only execution. In real-device evaluations on Android and HarmonyOS, our framework achieves action reuse ratios of 70.7-79.8% while maintaining over 2-fold execution speedup in most evaluated configurations.

title: Auto-Director: Leveraging Multi-Agent Collaboration for Autonomous Video Editing
summary: Autonomous video editing from open-world resources remains a challenging problem in multimedia content creation. Retrieval-based methods are constrained by fixed source material and lack creative flexibility, while generative models struggle with long-horizon coherence and often diverge from user intent. Both paradigms fail to replicate the structured, multi-stage reasoning that underlies professional post-production. To address these limitations, we present Auto-Director, a tool-augmented multi-agent framework that mirrors professional editorial workflows: a Planning Agent decomposes abstract topics into fact-grounded scripts via retrieval-augmented planning; a Material Agent indexes open-world footage through shot segmentation and visual tagging; an Editor Agent assembles semantically aligned clips with MLLM-driven spatial adaptation; and a Critic Agent governs an iterative Reflect-and-Revise loop that checks scene-level alignment and pacing. To rigorously evaluate this new paradigm, we introduce VEdit-Bench, a benchmark of 100 expert-curated topics with human-annotated Golden Scripts and a five-dimensional metric suite covering Narrative Logic, Factual Accuracy, Semantic Alignment, Compositional Quality, and Stylistic Cohesion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Auto-Director significantly outperforms baseline methods in both automated metrics and human evaluation, effectively bridging the gap between amateurs and professional-grade video production.

title: Asking Less, Adapting Better: Feedback-Efficient Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to follow instructions and navigate to target locations. However, current VLN agents often suffer severe performance degradation in unseen environments due to distribution shifts. Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) offers a promising paradigm to bridge this gap, yet existing methods that rely on unsupervised entropy minimization can propagate errors through the trajectory, causing cascading failures in navigation. Recent methods mitigate this by incorporating human feedback, but they apply trajectory-level supervision uniformly across all steps without localizing the actions is truly informative, leading to inefficient feedback utilization and mismatched optimization granularity. To address these limitations, we propose FETA, a Feedback-Efficient Test-Time Adaptation method that improves both feedback efficiency and optimization reliability. To reduce unnecessary human interventions, we introduce a hierarchical sample selection strategy to localize informative samples. Specifically, we first filter trajectories whose normalized policy entropy exhibits large fluctuations. Within each selected trajectory, we further select the critical action via an entropy-gradient saliency criterion and query a single binary feedback on its correctness. A discrepancy-aware entropy optimization objective then updates the policy only at the queried step, with adaptive scaling that assigns larger relative weights to samples with greater prediction-feedback discrepancy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FETA achieves state-of-the-art performance with fewer human interventions, while remaining robust under noisy feedback and continual adaptation settings.

title: NavBind: Diagnosing Instruction-Action Binding at Route Forks in Navigation VLAs
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) navigation models translate visual observations and instructions into actions. Navigation success assesses whether an agent reaches the goal. However, reaching the goal successfully does not establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions or relies on visual cues or navigation history. We introduce NavBind to diagnose instruction-action binding: whether changing the instruction influences the probabilistic distribution of the actions, with the navigation context fixed. We construct 3,252 route-fork contexts by recombining route-aligned instruction segments from R2R-CE and RxR-CE. Each context pairs full instructions that share the description of the route already traveled but specify different branches. Both are evaluated under the same agent state and navigation history. We compare generated local action sequences, the likelihoods of fixed reference action sequences under both instructions, and changes in visual attention and attribution. Across the evaluated models, higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions.

title: CODI: Improving Self-Supervised Vision Transformers with Cross Distillation
summary: Self-supervised Vision Transformers learn strong image-level representations, but their patch-level representations can be unreliable for dense prediction. We study this mismatch and find that the class token concentrates global semantics on a small number of representative patches, while dense prediction errors often occur on low-attention regions. We provide a local gradient analysis showing that, along the [CLS] attention readout, image-level self-distillation gradients are weighted by [CLS]-to-patch attention mass. To provide masked patches with global semantics without changing the architecture, we propose Cross Distillation (CODI), which mixes a small amount of the teacher class-token distribution into each teacher patch-token target. CODI gives every masked patch an attention-independent semantic correction while preserving the standard self-distillation architecture. Experiments on dense and image-level benchmarks show that CODI improves both dense and image-level performance under aligned pretraining settings. Code is available at https://github.com/EldercatSAM/CODI.

title: Experimental evidence of forward energy transfer induced by core-edge coupling in multiscale tokamak turbulence
summary: Turbulence in magnetically confined plasmas is inherently quasi-two-dimensional and can exhibit both inverse and forward energy transfer across scales. Experimental evidence for cross-scale energy transfer in the hot plasma core has, however, remained scarce. Understanding such energy transfer is crucial because it governs turbulent transport, which directly impacts confinement quality of fusion plasmas. Here we report experimental evidence consistent with forward energy transfer associated with core-edge coupling in tokamak turbulence. We combined multichannel collective Thomson scattering (CTS) and radially localized Doppler backscattering (DBS) to resolve cross-scale fluctuation dynamics. The results reveal that a quasi-coherent mode (QCM) originating from the edge is also present in the core and resonantly couples with broadband turbulence, producing significant forward energy transfer and characteristic secondary instabilities. These combined measurements indicate that quasi-two-dimensional tokamak turbulence can support a net energy transfer from ion to electron scales through cross-scale wave-wave interactions, contrary to the inverse cascade paradigm of idealized two-dimensional turbulence. Such a plasma regime is attractive for fusion reactors, as it avoids large edge-localized modes (ELMs) that damage first-wall components and maintains high confinement quality even in the presence of high-Z impurities.

title: What the Specification Did Not Say: Specification-Oracle Gaps in Test-Graded Coding-Agent Benchmarks
summary: Coding-agent benchmarks often describe a task in natural language but grade it with tests taken from the upstream project. Passing those tests can require information the description never states: a constant's name, a module path, an exact message. We call this a specification-oracle gap: where it exists, a benchmark also measures whether an agent reproduces upstream implementation details. We formalise the gap, including the inconsistencies that chains of dependent tasks add, and build a static audit for five languages that classifies every name-, path- and literal-level dependency of every scored test (held-out precision 89.2%, recall 92.9%). On SWE-Milestone (98 graded milestones, 35 published runs), 25 milestones contain a test that depends on an unstated, non-inferable name or path. Build units with such a dependency fail in 80.6% of runs, against 48.4% for comparable units without one, and withholding a single hidden name from the reference stops its unit's tests from compiling in 126 of 128 cases. The leaderboard's ranking is robust to removing the affected tests, but they shift scores within repositories and favour agents that reproduce upstream names. Across four further benchmarks, prevalence appears to follow construction: a third or more of the tasks are affected where specifications are release notes or LLM summaries, almost none where tasks are screened or written for their tests; how much a gap costs depends on how the harness grades. We release the audit, corrected filter lists and specification addenda.

title: Digital Twins of Networked Dynamical Systems: Machine Learning Prediction of Synchronization Transitions in Coupled Chaotic Oscillators
summary: Collective behaviors such as synchronization transitions are emergent properties of coupled oscillator systems, and how to reproduce them from data for large-scale systems remains an open problem. Here we propose a model-free coupled reservoir computing (CRC) architecture for constructing digital twins of coupled oscillator systems. The CRC decomposes the twin into three modules that mimic the nodal dynamics, the coupling function, and the coupling network, respectively, so that the modules can be reassembled for different coupled systems. Importantly, it is found that the trained CRC reproduces not only the collective states, including complete synchronization, phase synchronization, and chimera states, but also the synchronization transitions as the coupling strength varies, and the predicted collective behaviors are practically identical to those obtained by direct simulations of the original system. Moreover, the CRC is trained only on the time series of an isolated oscillator and of a pair of coupled oscillators, and the trained modules can be reused for different complex networks and for non-identical oscillators. Our findings establish the CRC architecture as a promising platform for digital twins of complex systems.

title: Large language models show systematic failures in incorporating evolving medical knowledge
summary: Medical knowledge evolves as clinical guidelines revise recommendations, yet whether large language models (LLMs) faithfully incorporate such changes remains unclear. We introduce ChronoEvo, comprising 1,709 recommendation-level revisions across 12 forms of medical knowledge change, to distinguish recognition of revised guidance from incorporation into clinical recommendations. In the primary model, 90.8% of responses recognized revisions and 80.2% were clinically correct, but only 58.5% fully incorporated guidance, yielding a 32.3-percentage-point recognition-incorporation gap. This dissociation persisted across 14 models and was corroborated by two clinicians' adjudicated assessment of 300 responses, yielding a 40.3-percentage-point gap in the validation sample. Changes in recommendation strength and patient eligibility were associated with retention of outdated guidance. A revision-salience intervention reduced outdated-content retention and improved clinical correctness but did not significantly improve full incorporation. These findings identify faithful incorporation of evolving medical knowledge as a distinct challenge for clinical LLM reliability, even when updated guideline evidence is available.

title: Future of Time Series Anomaly Detection: From Historical Review to Unified Outlook
summary: Time series anomaly detection (TSAD) is a foundational problem in data mining, aiming to identify observations that deviate significantly from nominal temporal patterns. Driven by escalating data volumes and application complexity, recent research has yielded diverse architectures, including diffusion models, state space models, and large language models (LLMs). However, existing surveys provide limited coverage of these emerging designs and lack a unified treatment of multivariate anomalies, cross-domain unified modeling, metric reliability, and contemporary evaluation challenges. To bridge these gaps, this survey delivers three core contributions: (1) We establish a refined anomaly categorization and a structured taxonomy of paradigms reflecting modern advances, comparing detection mechanisms and charting developmental trajectories across paradigms. (2) We provide an extensive analysis of evaluation methodologies and conduct comprehensive experiments to assess metric fidelity, complemented by an open-source benchmark repository encompassing algorithms, datasets, and evaluation tools. (3) We outline key open challenges, offering forward-looking perspectives on dynamic thresholding, model interpretability, zero-shot transfer, multi-modal alignment, and foundational models for time series. By addressing existing theoretical and empirical limitations, this survey establishes a coherent framework to guide future TSAD research and practical deployments.

title: Model-intrinsic, Weight-level, and Training-free Spectral Fingerprinting for Large Language Models
summary: The increasing release and reuse of Large Language Models (LLMs) as open-weight checkpoints make model fingerprinting important for ownership protection and offline auditing. Existing fingerprinting methods typically construct evidence from query responses, generated outputs, or input-induced activations. Although effective in representation-based settings, they can be affected by prompt selection, decoding configuration, inference environment, and forward-pass implementation, which may limit their applicability. Here we introduce a model-intrinsic weight-level framework that derives compact fingerprints from spectral structures encoded in LLM parameters. Specifically, the framework constructs GATE spectral scalar features from the singular-value distributions of GATE projection weights in gated feed-forward networks (FFNs), and aggregates the resulting layer-wise features through depth-wise segmented pooling to form a model-level fingerprint. Such representation preserves coarse layer-depth organization while reducing dependence on strict layer-to-layer alignment, enabling comparison across LLMs with different depths. The similarity between fingerprints is computed by linear centered kernel alignment. The entire pipeline is training-free and does not require input samples, generated outputs, forward activations, or an auxiliary verifier. Experiments on representative LLM families and post-training variants have demonstrated a clear separation between source-related models and unrelated ones, and stable similarity under instruction tuning, quantization, pruning, and distillation-related modifications, which verify that spectral features are robust evidence for LLM fingerprinting.

title: StochIKM: Automated High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Individual Patient Data from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves
summary: Individual patient data are the gold standard for secondary analysis of time-to-event evidence, but they are rarely released, and reconstruction from a published Kaplan-Meier figure could help. Existing methods all claim high fidelity, each judged by whichever agreements it happens to achieve, and each returns a single dataset although the map from figure to data is not bijective. We define fidelity explicitly: a dataset is admissible when it reproduces the risk table exactly, follows the digitized curve to within the image resolution, and respects the printed median, interval and event count. We propose StochIKM, a stochastic algorithm that digitizes the figure with a vision-capable language model and uses the high-fidelity definition as constraints, returning an admissible set of individual patient datasets. A solution is guaranteed to exist whenever the figure has been read correctly, so a failure indicts either the published figure or its digitization. In simulation and in 79 arms from published oncology trials, StochIKM reproduces the published risk tables and medians more closely than LLM-improved IPDfromKM, a high-impact alternative.

title: MBABench-2.0: Evaluating AI Agents on Constructing Financial Spreadsheets Beyond Simple Verifiability
summary: Spreadsheets are the lingua franca of modern finance, driving valuation, forecast, audit, and many other core workflows of the industry. As LLM agents advance to automate knowledge work, spreadsheet construction is a natural and pertinent testbed. However, most existing spreadsheet benchmarks evaluate agents on fill-in-the-blank style tasks, where an agent performs minor edits in otherwise complete spreadsheets. This protocol fails to capture the most central and time-consuming part of the spreadsheet workflow: the modeling decisions, format design, and sheet layout regular knowledge workers need to toil through to build a workbook from scratch. We introduce MBABench-2.0, a benchmark of 101 original spreadsheet construction tasks, the hardest of which is estimated to take 33 hours for a modeler with 3+ years of experience. Unlike coding or math, where a unit test or a final answer can verify an agent's output, the quality of a financial spreadsheet that concerns readability, maintainability, or auditability, is not so simply verifiable. To holistically evaluate spreadsheet construction, we introduce 129 criteria spanning 12 categories that operationalize quality beyond the accuracy of the spreadsheet. Evaluating over 20 agents across 8 models and 4 harness types, we find that frontier agents rarely construct spreadsheets that are both accurate and meet our quality criteria: the top agent achieves a pass rate of only 16% on the benchmark. The benchmark demonstrates a substantial gap in spreadsheet building capability of current agents.

title: Rethinking Underwater Image Enhancement: Learning through Text-Guided Degradation Curriculum
summary: Existing paired clean-degraded datasets have advanced learning-based underwater image enhancement, but they remain either limited in scale or difficult to acquire, and still fail to adequately cover the diverse degradations encountered in real-world underwater environments. Such scarce and insufficient data ultimately restrict the generalization of underwater image enhancement models, highlighting the need for realistic and controllable degradation modeling to better capture real underwater conditions and improve enhancement robustness. To this end, we propose a unified degradation-aware training framework for the underwater image enhancement task. A Text-Conditioned Degradation Augmentation Pipeline uses a text-guided diffusion model to synthesize diverse and semantically consistent degraded samples, providing paired data to support the subsequent curriculum learning strategy. The proposed Progressive Degradation Curriculum organizes training across multiple attributes and difficulty levels to promote balanced learning, and a Transmission-Guided One-Step Diffusion Model leverages this progressive process to better address the wide range of degradation severity and restoration ambiguity in underwater images. Extensive experiments on multiple underwater benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed method achieves superior performance. Our code and models will be released upon the publication of this work.

title: Better Reasoning, Not Just Bigger Models: A Structure-Grounded Framework for Efficient and Reliable Inference
summary: Scaling large language models has substantially improved linguistic fluency, yet reliable autonomous agents require more than fluent generation. In multi-turn inference, current agentic systems often produce semantically plausible but structurally ungrounded reasoning, especially under incomplete observations. We propose Structure-Grounded Uncertainty Reduction (SGUR), a training-free framework that complements token-level generation with active uncertainty reduction over structured hypothesis spaces. SGUR represents incomplete observations as a query graph and aligns them with candidate hypothesis graphs through a prior-weighted partial graph matching mechanism, where database-derived empirical priors assign greater importance to decision-relevant relations rather than treating all graph edges uniformly. The resulting inference state is iteratively refined by an active information-gain strategy that selects the next most informative node to query, systematically pruning the candidate space. We instantiate SGUR on a challenging PrimeKG-derived sequential medical diagnosis benchmark, demonstrating that structural grounding can partially substitute for model scale: starting from only two observed symptoms, SGUR achieves 92.5% Hit@3, outperforming the strongest Graph-RAG baseline by 9.4 percentage points while using approximately 5x fewer tokens. Notably, SGUR enables smaller backbone models to match or exceed the performance of models up to 10x larger, suggesting that structural grounding provides a more robust and efficient paradigm for scaling agent performance than relying exclusively on increasing model size.

title: Compact-Bench: Measuring What Context Compaction Costs Long-Horizon Coding Agents
summary: Context compaction lets long-horizon coding agents continue beyond their context windows, but can erase the state needed to finish a task. Prior evaluations measure efficiency, retained information, or end-to-end success, leaving the effect of a specific history replacement difficult to isolate. Compact-Bench pairs full-history and summary-only continuations from a shared repository state, and evaluates recurring details and successive production compactions. It covers 35 SWE-bench repairs, 146 agentic sessions, and 106 production chains. Across 14 summarizer backbones, stable damage ranges from 5-64% of 22 full-history successes: Claude Opus 4.8 preserves the most repairs, while DeepSeek-Flash damages the most. With Kimi-K3 as summarizer, the Kimi Code prompt preserves the most task continuations (19/22), whereas Claude Code retains the most recurring details (15.0%). LLM summaries retain at most 16.0% of recurring details, compared with 79.1% for mechanical extraction; production summaries retain 15.7% at the first boundary. Failures recur across methods: one repair is damaged by 13/14 backbones, and another by all 5 prompts. These results show that reliable compaction requires preserving the progress needed to complete a task, and that retaining relevant information alone does not ensure successful continuation. Code is available at https://github.com/cai-jianfeng/compact-bench and data is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/caijanfeng/compact-bench.

title: CMAR-search: Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning for Object Search in Dynamic Interactive Environments
summary: Dynamic interactive object search in large-scale human environments presents substantial challenges for existing methods. Current scene representations like 3D Scene Graphs (3DSG) only provide coarse-grained spatial segmentation and cannot identify functional areas such as storage or leisure areas. Without functional area understanding, existing methods are constrained to exhaustive sequential exploration at large scales, resulting in inefficient search behaviors -- particularly in open-layout environments with numerous interactive objects such as drawers and cabinets. Moreover, these methods lack adaptability to environmental dynamics such as object relocations. To address these limitations, this paper proposes CMAR-search, a novel framework built upon Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning (CMAR). Our approach leverages commonsense about area functionalities and aggregates environmental memory to construct a Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG), which organizes the environment into functional areas with their associated containers. Through this structured representation, CMAR enables hierarchical action planning at both macro-area and micro-container levels, empowering the system to efficiently identify and inspect semantically relevant areas for effective object search. Notably, CMAR continuously integrates real-time perception, accumulated memory, and commonsense to dynamically relocalize objects in changing environments. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that CMAR-search significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in both success rate and search efficiency for object search in dynamic interactive environments.

title: PATH: Preference-Aware Traversability Estimation for Robotic Teleoperation in Off-Road Navigation
summary: Traversability estimation is critical for ground vehicle teleoperation, yet existing methods often neglect the human operator's preferences for speed and risk tolerance. To address this gap, we propose PATH-Net, a Preference-Aware Traversability estimation Hierarchical Network that adaptively generates preference-conditioned traversability cost maps and speed profiles for off-road teleoperation. Our framework integrates visual and geometric bird's-eye-view features with short-term historical vehicle states through a multi-head shared-backbone architecture. Our PATH-Net infers traversability cost maps while optimizing speed recommendations by using maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning and sparse speed supervision. Our method incorporates operator preference via an asymmetric feature aggregation mechanism, splitting inference into a cost branch that prioritizes high-risk traversability regions and a speed branch that outputs preference-adjusted recommended speeds. Experiments with 15 operators across 225 teleoperated trajectories show alignment with user-specific navigation strategies, achieving modified Hausdorff distance of 0.17 m (aggressive) and 0.15 m (conservative). In the questionnaire assessment, participants reported lower NASA-TLX workload scores with PATH-Net recommendations than without recommendations, decreasing from 34.7 to 22.2. These results support preference-conditioned trajectory and speed recommendation for off-road teleoperation.

title: HiMark: Hierarchical and Controllable Multi-bit Watermarking for Large Language Models
summary: With the rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) in text generation applications, it has become increasingly difficult to trace generated content and assign responsibility for its use, raising concerns about provenance, copyright protection, and accountability. Multi-bit watermarking addresses these issues by embedding multi-bit provenance information into generated text, but reliable extraction remains difficult due to sparse per-bit evidence and the trade-off between watermark-extraction accuracy and text quality. To deal with these challenges, we propose HiMark, a hierarchical and controllable multi-bit watermarking framework for LLM-generated text. During watermark embedding, HiMark uses a hierarchical candidate-control mechanism, including initial candidate sampling, layer-wise tournament elimination, support-based refinement, and support-threshold filtering. During watermark detection, a model-agnostic evidence aggregation mechanism computes multi-layer support evidence for each observed token, and then accumulates these token-level votes into the corresponding information for robust watermark extraction. Experiments show that HiMark improves watermark extraction accuracy while maintaining text quality, e.g., the watermark extraction accuracy is 90.01% under the paraphrasing attack when 32 bits were embedded within a text containing 300 tokens, demonstrating its effectiveness for provenance tracking.

title: Detection of Solar-like Oscillations and Granulation at Infrared Wavelengths using JWST
summary: Stellar oscillations and granulation are key probes of stellar convection, one of the most poorly understood processes in stars. Stellar models predict strong wavelength dependence of the amplitudes of oscillations and granulation, but hitherto both processes have only been measured at optical wavelengths. Here we present the first detection of oscillations and granulation at infrared wavelengths, using JWST time-series observations of the F6V main-sequence star WASP-121 that were obtained to study the atmosphere of an exoplanet. We find that the amplitudes of oscillations and granulation decrease with wavelength, consistent with expectations, but with a functional form that deviates from simple blackbody scaling. The detection opens the door to detailed tests of 3D convection models, facilitates the combined modeling of stellar and exoplanet signals in JWST passbands for exoplanet observations, and supports the predicted asteroseismic yields from the infrared time-domain data that will soon be obtained by the Roman Space Telescope.

title: TT-SAX: A Two-Track Time Series Symbolization for Natural Language Shape Querying
summary: Natural language querying for time series databases aims to let users find what they need in long histories of data by asking in plain language. Shape queries ask how a series moves. They are the main challenge of this task. Recent work makes them feasible by using symbolization as a bridge between the query and the long history. However, existing symbolizations were designed for compression, similarity indexing, or classification. What a symbolization should provide for natural language querying has not been systematically studied. We therefore examine the definitions of six classical symbolizations against this task and identify three limitations. (1) Direction is missing from the string, (2) direction is measured at too small a scale, and (3) the letters are arbitrary. Three design principles follow. We follow these principles and make a minimal redesign of SAX called TT-SAX (two-track SAX). The level letters stay. Each segment gains a trend letter. It is measured across neighboring segments rather than inside one, and graded to match the adjectives that queries use. We conduct extensive experiments on the public NLQTSBench benchmark, comparing TT-SAX with the six classical symbolizations across six LLMs. TT-SAX outperforms all six on shape queries, and ablations trace its gains back to the three limitations one by one. This paper is the first systematic study of time series symbolization with natural language querying as the design goal. It provides a foundation for future research on this task. Our code is available at https://github.com/Atlamtiz/tt-sax.

title: Visual Grounding First, Multimodal In-context Learning Follows
summary: LLMs have shown strong in-context learning (ICL) capability, but extending it to Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) remains challenging. Prior multimodal ICL methods often rely on ICL-specific datasets for additional training or task vector extraction, which can improve performance on the same ICL benchmark used for adaptation. However, they do not generalize well to other benchmarks and often induce forgetting in previously well-solved tasks. For this reason, we identify 'visual grounding' as the key bottleneck in multimodal ICL; MLLMs often fail to attend to task-relevant visual evidence in demonstrations, instead over-relying on textual cues and producing hallucinated outputs. To address this, we propose ProCoRe to enhance visual grounding through contrastive reinforcement learning on multimodal contrastive data for improving multimodal ICL. ProCoRe generates captions for contrastive image pairs, decomposes them into propositions, and optimizes contrastive rewards that encourage alignment with corresponding images while discouraging mismatched ones. Despite never seeing ICL-formatted training examples, ProCoRe improves average multimodal ICL classification accuracy by 5.6% and captioning ROUGE-L by 13.8% over the off-the-shelf Qwen-VL-3-8B model, outperforming ICL-data-dependent state of the arts across benchmarks. Finally, we introduce PICL, a personalized multimodal ICL captioning benchmark that tests whether MLLMs genuinely understand visual demonstrations rather than relying on pre-trained semantic priors.

title: Supercoiling Drives DNA-Protein Co-Condensation
summary: The co-condensation of DNA and proteins plays an important role in genome compaction, including heterochromatin formation and chromosome segregation. Meanwhile, transcription and replication continuously generate DNA supercoiling, yet how the resulting torsional stress affects co-condensation remains poorly understood. Here, by coupling DNA elasticity to a protein concentration field, we show that supercoiling acts as a topological catalyst for co-condensation through a mutually reinforcing interplay with protein wetting. Specifically, protein wetting facilitates twist-to-writhe conversion, generating highly writhed DNA conformations that in turn promote capillary collapse into a protein-rich droplet. In the absence of supercoiling, DNA remains kinetically trapped in metastable extended states within our model, whereas sufficiently strong supercoiling removes the nucleation barrier and enables spontaneous co-condensation. These results establish topology as a distinct control parameter for biomolecular condensation and provide a mechanical framework for how active genomic processes can dynamically regulate large-scale genome organization.

title: DagFlow AI: Agentic Synthetic Data Generation for Personalized Statistics Learning
summary: To provide personalized learning experiences in courses that teach data analysis skills, instructors often search for datasets that appeal to a student's interests, align with specific learning objectives, and are appropriate for the student's skill level. Datasets that match all three criteria can be difficult to find. DagFlow-AI is an agentic AI data generation tool that creates realistic, synthetic datasets tailored to these criteria.
